en: The Scripture on the Moon-Lamp Samādhi Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle; also known as the Scripture on the Ten Practices of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Song Dynasty Śramaṇa Xian-gong.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
In the garden, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, sixty thousand bodhisattvas, and an incalculable number of devas and humans,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was seated within that gathering.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Young man, there are ten matters concerning the bodhisattva’s practice of giving."
What are the ten? First, truly eliminating the mind of envy;
second, constantly giving with a pure mind.
Third, hundreds of thousands of people cannot deprive him of his wealth;
fourth, he will not die before attaining the unsurpassed excellence;
fifth, he will be born into a family of great nobility and wealth.
Sixth, one is fond of giving in whatever place one is born;
seventh, one is cherished and remembered by the fourfold assembly;
eighth, one is free from fear, entering assemblies without hindrance, and the sound of one’s name is heard throughout the ten directions.
Ninth, his hands and feet are soft and supple;
tenth, he always delights in spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) until he sits beneath the Bodhi tree. O Youth!
"These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s practice of giving.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Having already distanced oneself from envy, One whose mind always delights in giving;
Though they pass away while possessing the most excellent things, they are reborn immediately into a family of great wealth.
In whatever place they are born, their minds are always joyful, and they delight in the practice of giving;
they are beloved and remembered by all beings, whether they live as householders or have gone forth to study.
Fearless in the midst of the great assembly, he encounters no doubt or difficulty wherever he goes;
his fame is heard afar, throughout the provinces, kingdoms, districts, and towns.
Their hands and feet are always supple, and whatever they desire is no longer difficult to obtain;
they immediately gain spiritual friends: the Buddhas and their disciples.
Never again shall they give rise to thoughts of envy; their minds will always delight in the desire to practice giving.
By maintaining such supreme excellence until the end of life, they will act without envy in all their deeds.
He is immediately born into a family of great wealth and nobility, his mind always joyful as he practices giving;
beloved by many hundreds of millions of people—such is the conduct of one who delights in generosity.
It is no longer difficult to find virtuous friends; one constantly beholds the Buddhas and their disciples.
Having seen them, one immediately delights in making offerings to them; such is the practice of those who practice giving.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding the pure observance of precepts by a bodhisattva. What are these ten?

First, to fulfill one's vows; second, to study the Buddha-way; third, to always honor and delight in wisdom; fourth, not to speak falsely even at the point of death; fifth, not to turn back in resolve when seeing the world; sixth, to abandon birth and death; seventh, to seek nirvana; eighth, to practice in solitude and stillness; ninth, to attain samādhi; and tenth, to practice without poverty.
"Young man!
These are the ten matters of pure observance of the precepts for a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Thus they fulfill their aspirations, training in the path and conduct of all Buddhas;
always delighting in supreme wisdom, they are never subject to fear."
No longer turning back from their vows, nor wavering in their careful cultivation of all practices;
always casting far away birth and death, they seek the path to Nirvāṇa.
Always practicing in solitary places, one immediately attains samādhi;
never experiencing poverty, one is established in the category of ethical discipline.
That person shall immediately fulfill all their aspirations; this bodhisattva trains in the path of all Buddhas.
The wise one does not boast before others; such is that person’s purity of precepts.
The resolve he maintains is exceedingly firm and no longer difficult; he shall never again waver from what he has undertaken.
Having seen the countless evils of birth and death, he immediately abandons them to seek the path to Nirvana.
Their minds no longer cling to thoughts; such persons establish themselves with firm precepts.
They attain a pure buddha-field without exception; those who possess pure precepts have such conduct.
The Buddha said to the youth:
"There are ten matters by which a bodhisattva establishes patience. What are these ten?

First, fire cannot burn them; second, blades cannot harm them; third, poisons cannot take effect upon them; fourth, water cannot drown them; fifth, non-human beings protect them; sixth, they obtain the adornment of their physical marks; seventh, all evil paths are closed off to them; eighth, it is not difficult for them to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven; ninth, they attain peace and security day and night; tenth, their bliss and happiness are unshakable.
"O youth! These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva abides in patience.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Fire cannot burn that person, nor can a blade inflict harm;
poison cannot take effect upon them, nor can water sweep them away."
All non-human beings shall protect them, and they will immediately attain the thirty-two marks;
they shall block all evil paths—such is the virtue of those who practice patience.
Though he sought among the Brahmās and Śakras, they too could not be easily attained;
yet he constantly attained the practice of peace and security, fully awakening to the reality of impermanence.
Neither sword nor fire can wound them; they cannot be harmed even when walking amidst poison.
Protected by devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits—such is the practice of those who possess patience.
One attains the thirty-two marks in this very body; such a person no longer fears the evil realms.
Upon death, they are reborn in the Brahma Heaven; for those who practice a mind of loving-kindness, this is the path.
Day and night they attain peaceful conduct; always delighting in joy, their bodies achieve stability.
With pure minds toward all that exists, they never harbor intentions of anger or malice.
The Buddha told the youth:
"There are ten matters regarding the diligence of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?

First, they possess majestic spiritual power; second, they are protected by all Buddhas; third, non-human beings likewise protect them; fourth, having heard the Dharma, they never again forget it; fifth, they hear teachings not previously heard; sixth, they attain lofty and brilliant wisdom; seventh, they attain various samādhis; eighth, they are ultimately free from illness; ninth, they find peace and stability in their eating and drinking; tenth, they attain a suppleness like that of an *utpala* flower, being neither rigid nor coarse.
"O youth! These are the ten matters for a bodhisattva practicing with diligence.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Always possessing majestic spiritual power, one shall never again transgress into various evils;
all non-human beings will protect them, and they shall swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha."
Having heard the Dharma of the sutras, they do not forget it; those who have not yet heard it seek and attain it.
Such a person immediately attains high wisdom; those who are diligent possess such virtue.
One attains the practice of all samādhis and shall never suffer from illness;
the diligent one, endowed with wisdom, shall attain the practice of the Buddha-way.
Through the food one consumes, one attains peace and security, and immediately engages in the practice of vigor;
just as the utpala flower in water gradually grows and reaches full maturity.
The pure and white dharmas are likewise; they cause the bodhisattva to gradually achieve completion.
No one can ever withstand them, as he attains a place of peace and bliss in heaven.
The Tathāgata’s practice of diligent progress transcends countless eons through such exertion;
he has fully explained all that the Bodhisattvas cultivate and uphold through their diligent efforts.
Those who possess such diligence have majestic spiritual power and are constantly protected by all Buddhas;
as they all receive and uphold this practice of the Way, those people will attain the Buddha-way before long.
What one has heard will never again be forgotten, and one further attains other various dharmas and practices;
the wisdom of such a person gradually increases—this is the case for those who practice with diligence.
Various samādhis constantly increase within them; they shall never suffer from illness.
Whatever food and drink they may consume, all shall bring them peace and security.
Day and night they accomplish pure conduct, The diligent never know rest;
Such a person will soon swiftly attain Buddhahood— Thus is the one who practices diligence honored.
The Buddha said to the youth:
"There are ten practices for a bodhisattva who practices dhyāna. What are these ten?"

First, exclusive practice and abiding; second, performing the deeds of the Path; third, being free from fear and difficulty; fourth, correctly and truly regulating the sense faculties; fifth, being beloved by others; sixth, distancing oneself from desire; seventh, not wavering from a single-minded focus; eighth, liberation from the realm of Māra; ninth, dwelling in the realm of the Buddha; tenth, attaining liberation.
"Young man!
These are the ten practices of a bodhisattva who sits in meditation.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke these verses:
That person does not turn back from their practice; this is precisely abiding in the practice of the Truths.
Devoting themselves exclusively to the affairs of the various paths, that person abandons improper conduct.
In what he cultivates, there is no further attachment; his faculties are already tranquil and settled.
He has thus attained peace and joy, sitting in contemplation of the practices of the Way.
That person, having already departed from craving and desire, sits in peace with a unified mind;
by remaining far removed from the realm of Māra, they immediately abide in the realm of the Buddha.
The practitioner who possesses this upholding, who alone delights among the trees,
immediately attains the practice of liberation and thereby achieves the ten phrases of attainment.
That Bodhisattva abides in non-action and does not engage in it; he completely abandons all that is improper to practice.
Having discarded incorrect conduct, he delights in correct conduct; such is the state of one who contemplates samādhi.
That person will never again have moments of greedy attachment; the wise who practice with tranquility are not covetous.
With body and mind well-awakened, they maintain the precepts; those who practice samādhi possess these qualities.
Walking among the trees in emptiness, he has no fear; such a person never again clings to greed.
All non-human beings cherish and protect him, as he thus remains far removed from desire and wanders alone.
Never clinging to desire nor being greedy, one thus escapes the realm of Māra;
abiding instead in the realm of the Tathāgata, such a person is ultimately liberated from all that is perverse.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā. What are these ten?
First, to give away all that one possesses as alms without any expectation of reward;
second, to no longer violate the precepts and not to use the precepts for self-adornment;
third, to abide in the power of patience while dwelling without the notion of a person.
Fourth, practicing diligence without craving for body or life;
fifth, practicing dhyāna without dwelling in dhyāna;
sixth, subduing the evil Māras.
Seventh, he cannot be moved by the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths;
eighth, he personally knows birth and death;
ninth, he possesses a compassionate mind toward sentient beings.
Tenth, not seeking disciples or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Young man, these are the ten matters for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The person's giving is equal toward all, And they do not harbor thoughts of expecting a reward;
They protect the sutras and precepts, not daring to transgress them, Nor do they have any attachment to seeking."
Practicing patience and wisdom, one ultimately has no conception of a person;
seeing others, one exerts diligence, with body, will, and mind free from attachment.
Practicing single-mindedness and wisdom, Abiding nowhere and free from conceptualization;
Having subdued all demons, The wise possess such virtues.
Among the ninety-six kinds of paths, none are able to cause him to waver;
having attained the knowledge that brings an end to birth and death, such is the state of the wise one.
Toward all sentient beings, they possess the practice of great compassion;
toward disciples and pratyekabuddhas, they do not dwell upon their own sought-after practices.
Giving all things without expectation, Not transgressing the precepts and not dwelling on evil;
Practicing patience without the notion of a self— These are the deeds of one who honors wisdom.
Diligence consists in dwelling in secluded places; in meditation, there is neither conceptualization nor abiding.
Such a person uses wisdom to subdue Māra; these are the qualities of one who practices wisdom.
The various non-Buddhists cannot move him; that person thus understands birth and death.
He feels compassion for the multitude of people; such are the qualities of one who practices wisdom.
The various disciples and pratyekabuddhas never harbor thoughts of seeking anything from him;
such is the dwelling of one on the Buddha-way, for this is the practice of those who cultivate wisdom.
The Buddha said to the youth:
"A bodhisattva of great wisdom has ten types of practice. What are these ten?"

First, knowing the evil paths; second, knowing the wholesome paths; third, resolving matters of doubt; fourth, manifesting the direct path for others; fifth, abandoning the evil paths; sixth, abiding in the right path; seventh, being at the gate of the deathless (*amṛta*); eighth, attaining the seat beneath the Bodhi tree; ninth, manifesting the path of illumination for sentient beings; and tenth, having no fear of the evil paths.
"Young man! These are the ten practices of a bodhisattva of great wisdom.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"To understand all afflictions and to fully comprehend these two matters;
such a person then abandons affliction and immediately follows the practice of the Buddha-way."
With wisdom, one resolves all doubts and immediately manifests the reality of direct vision;
thus abandoning the conduct of the evil realms, one immediately comes to abide in the right path.
Seeing that one dwells within the gate of the Deathless, one then attains sitting beneath the Bodhi tree;
for the sake of the people, one manifests and explains the truth, causing them not to fear the various evil realms.
Thoroughly understanding the countless phenomena of worldly toil, and knowing that these two matters are thus,
such a person abandons worldly toil and learns the sublime Dharma therein.
To resolve the doubts of all people, one thereby attains the vision of the virtuous and upright;
immediately casting aside the affairs of the evil realms, the one of great wisdom abides forever on the Path.
Always dwelling at the gate of the deathless nectar, One sits beneath the immeasurable Bodhi tree;
Manifesting light for immeasurable billions of people, Such a person shall never fear the evil realms.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters for a bodhisattva who upholds the supreme Dharma-gift and bestows the Dharma upon others. What are these ten?

First, abandoning evil; second, practicing goodness; third, becoming a true sage; fourth, purifying one’s buddha-field; fifth, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; sixth, bestowing all manner of requisites through giving; seventh, subduing all afflictions; eighth, bestowing wisdom upon all people; ninth, practicing a mind of loving-kindness; and tenth, attaining a peaceful mind in the present life.
"O Youth! These are the ten matters by which a bodhisattva maintains the noble gift of Dharma and bestows that gift of Dharma upon others.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Abandon all unwholesome states, and fully practice all wholesome deeds;
abide in the wisdom of the Dharma, and always delight in the mind of giving."
He shall purify his Buddha-field and immediately attain the unsurpassed realm;
he shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree and bestow the gift of Dharma like a precious jewel.
By giving away all that one possesses, one trains as a King of Dharma;
thus distancing oneself from all worldly defilements, such a person will not find it difficult to attain Buddhahood.
Bestowing gifts upon all people, he always maintains the practice of a compassionate heart;
being free from the conduct of envy, he brings peace and security to non-human beings.
One of great wisdom abandons all that is unwholesome; such a person always dwells securely in the wholesome.
Firmly established in the Noble Dharma, they cannot be shaken; the one of great wisdom is ever conjoined with the Dharma.
One will thus constantly attain a pure land and always practice the deeds of the Buddha-way;
one will always dwell beneath the Bodhi tree—such are the benefits for those who promote the gift of Dharma.
Free from the defilements of worldly toil, they give to the multitude; They immediately come to understand the affairs of their own bodies;
Fully liberated from all worldly matters, Such persons shall ultimately have no obstructions whatsoever.
That person, knowing this for themselves, resolves their mind to practice such giving for the sake of all people;
possessing a heart of loving-kindness, they are free from envy, and seeing that all phenomena are peaceful, they realize there is no self.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding the bodhisattva’s practice of emptiness. What are these ten?

First, practicing the Buddha-way; second, practicing without attachment; third, not aspiring for rebirth; fourth, not violating the precepts; fifth, not slandering the worthy; sixth, not engaging in contentious conduct; seventh, non-attainment; eighth, practicing the path alone; ninth, not disputing with the Buddhas; and tenth, practicing the acceptance of the Dharma.
"Young man! This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice the ten matters of emptiness.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“The conduct practiced by those superior persons leads to the attainment of the world of the Most Honored One;
the courageous practice therein, where no life-force can be apprehended.”
They do not cling to any worlds, but sit peacefully in meditative contemplation;
they do not aspire for any rebirths, and thus clearly understand all dharmas as empty.
Never again shall they transgress the rules of discipline; upholding the precepts, they remain beyond reproach.
Throughout their lives, they never speak ill of others, nor do they slander other worthy ones.
One who practices the Path without contention will never have any disputes;
they understand all matters as they truly are and practice accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
Even unto the loss of their very lives, they shall never slander the World-Honored One;
having accumulated all dharmas, they preserve themselves with minds free from fear.
In all worlds, the Buddha-way is inconceivable;
They uphold all the Buddhas' teachings And no longer doubt the dharma of emptiness.
The conduct of such a person is supreme and sublime; they do not abide among the various non-Buddhist paths.
Their practice of dhyāna is peaceful and free from attachment; in all things, there is neither life-force nor a person.
Such a person will ultimately have no greedy attachment; one who practices single-mindedness has no conceptualizations.
Because they know there is no person and no self-dharma, they ultimately have no further aspirations.
Fully understanding the principles of all phenomena as empty, they never become attached to what is used by the multitude;
such a person is forever free from thoughts of craving and attachment, maintaining a mind of pure faith toward the Buddha at all times.
Such a person will never have disputes or litigation; dwelling alone and practicing, they find fulfillment in solitude.
Such a person abides in the path of the Buddha and upholds all the teachings of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding the practice of a bodhisattva dwelling in solitude. What are these ten?

First, having a pure intention; second, being free from desire; third, mindfulness of all Buddhas; fourth, practice through faith; fifth, non-doubt regarding wisdom; sixth, returning repeatedly to all Buddhas; seventh, not slandering the Dharma; eighth, practice in solitude; ninth, attaining disciplined abiding; and tenth, the four analytical knowledges of wisdom.
"O youth! These are the ten practices for a bodhisattva dwelling in solitude.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Ultimately free from the conduct of desire, always possessing a pure intention;
one then honors the state of desirelessness, practicing with a single mind in solitary retreat."
One who contemplates the light of the entire world will transform that thought into faith;
having no doubt regarding this singular wisdom, one realizes that the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
If one shows gratitude toward the Buddhas, the Buddhas will never abandon the Dharma;
by immediately practicing the conduct of tranquility, one then abides in the Dharma of stillness.
That person immediately attains understanding of the matter, and alone finds joy among the trees;
having cast aside wealth and profit, they practice the Path in solitude.
That person shall immediately possess a pure mind, constantly abandoning all evil deeds;
their conduct will be tranquil and unsurpassed, and they shall never again doubt the wisdom of the Buddhas.
That person contemplates the Buddha’s unsurpassed state, And practices with faith the conduct of the God among Gods;
Furthermore, they no longer doubt the wisdom of the Buddhas— Such are the qualities of one who practices in profound stillness.
One shows reciprocal gratitude toward all superiors, and never again abandons the practice of the Dharma;
for one who practices in solitude there is stillness, and for one who dwells in seclusion these qualities arise.
They shall immediately attain the ground of sublime truth and tranquility, and swiftly comprehend all matters of realization;
they will constantly expound countless sutras, and that person shall never encounter any hindrance.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding the practice of a bodhisattva dwelling in seclusion. What are these ten?

First is the practice of tranquility; second, staying far removed from the multitude; third, being free from contention; fourth, being free from anger; fifth, not entering into various conditioned activities; sixth, not entering into the offenses of others; seventh, recollecting the matter of liberation; eighth, practicing with a peaceful and single-minded focus; ninth, swiftly realizing the realization of liberation; and tenth, attaining samādhi by virtue of non-attachment.
"Young man! These are the ten matters of the noble practice for a bodhisattva in solitary retreat.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Always feeling a sense of solitude, one should then distance oneself from the assembly of people;
never engaging in disputes or contention, one should practice alone."
Always free from thoughts of anger, never turning back to attachment toward the realms;
no longer engaging in disputes or litigation—one who dwells in seclusion possesses such virtue.
One thus practices the conduct of tranquility, constantly dwelling in solitary practice;
thereupon, through the matter of liberation, one swiftly attains transcendence.
Sitting alone in a secluded place above, he constantly abandons the company of the wicked;
such a person never enters into the transgressions of others—this is the nature of one who sits among the trees.
One then grows weary of all birth and death; such a person has no craving for various worldly objects, nor do they have any cause for fear, as they sit beneath a tree.
Never engaging in disputes or litigation with others, he always delights in solitude and tranquility;
constantly guarding his body, speech, and mind, his virtues are beyond measure when he dwells in seclusion.
One immediately attains the state of sublime liberation, And is well-seated in the samādhi of stillness;
Practicing the conduct of tranquility amidst the trees, Those dwelling in secluded places possess such virtues.
The Buddha said to the youth:
“There are ten matters regarding the bodhisattva’s practice of begging for alms. What are these ten?
First, one does not wish for others to know of one's conduct;
second, one does not cause others to know of one's merit;
third, one does not desire wealth or profit.
Fourth, not having self-proclamation nor being flatteringly insincere;
fifth, abiding in the path of the noble ones;
sixth, not speaking of one's own merits.
Seventh, not seeking satisfaction from others;
eighth, neither rejoicing nor grieving when visiting the homes of others;
ninth, setting aside material gifts of food and clothing to bestow the gift of the Dharma upon others.
Tenth, he dwells in virtue without flattery or deceit, taking only from that which is given as a gift of Dharma. Young man,
these are the ten matters in which a bodhisattva dwells while practicing for alms, dwelling in virtue without flattery or deceit.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"He does not wish for his practice to be known, Nor does he cling to the deeds he performs;
Equal-minded toward gain and loss, Such a person abides in the teaching."
Nor does one commit offenses against the noble ones; there is no conduct of flattery or praise-seeking.
One does not speak of one's own virtues, nor does one speak of the faults of others.
Neither sorrowful nor lacking in joy, he preaches the Dharma free from concern for food and clothing;
all that he says brings delight—such is the virtue of one who wanders for alms.
Not desiring praise nor seeking fame, they always abide in the practice of the four noble ones;
without flattery or deceit for the sake of wealth and profit, such is the conduct of those who receive the teachings.
One does not praise oneself nor speak of others' faults; from the outset, one never speaks ill of those with malicious tongues.
Hearing of another's merits, one always rejoices; such a mendicant knows contentment and moderation.
Free from attachment to food and clothing, he excellently bestows the gift of Dharma; He also does not seek after wealth or profit.
All virtuous people rejoice in what he says; Such are the qualities of one who receives the Honored One’s teaching.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, seventy-two thousand people resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the youth Mañjuśrī, along with the entire assembly of devas, nāgas, and worldly humans, were filled with joy; they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, one fascicle: this is the translation of the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* by the late Master Dan from the Imperial Canon (Danzang). However, its wording and meaning differ significantly from the version in the Song edition of the Tripitaka held in that region; it is not yet known which is correct.
According to the *Kaiyuan lu*, there are two distinct translations of this sutra:
first, among those for which the translation exists but the manuscript does not, there is one fascicle translated by An Shigao of the Later Han;
second, among those for which both the translation and the manuscript exist, there is one fascicle translated by the Sramana Xian Gong of the Song dynasty.
All state: "Extracted from the seventh fascicle of the *Mahācandrapradīpa-sūtra*.
Under the catalog of his late father’s translations, it is annotated as follows:
"The Scripture on the Tenfold Practice of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī";
furthermore, regarding its length, it states:
"one scroll of ten sheets."
Now, upon examining this manuscript of the *Dānapāramitā-sūtra*, from the Six Perfections down to the Alms-round (*piṇḍapāta*), it covers twelve topics in total, each explained through ten points;

furthermore, as for its length, it consists of twelve lines per page on what was formerly a ten-page scroll—thus we know this is truly the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra* translated by the former master [Dharmakṣema].
However, the Record states:
"Extracted from the seventh fascicle of the Great Sūtra"; yet upon consulting the text now, it is found in the first half of the sixth fascicle, which does not correspond [with that statement].
Do you suspect that there is a discrepancy between the ancient and modern versions regarding the division of fascicles?
Or perhaps it is merely a scribal error where "six" was written as "seven"!
